name: solve-js-testing
description: Testing patterns, shared utilities, and conventions for solve-js test suites
prompt:
You are working on the solve-js project. These are the testing rules and conventions:

## Shared Test Utilities
All tests import from tools/testUtils.ts — NOT from each other.
- createEngine(locale?, diagnostic?) → fresh ExpressionEngine
- evalExpr(engine, expr, lineNum?) → Value
- evalDoc(engine, doc) → ParsingResult
- tokenize(input) → filtered Token[]
- expectApproximately(actual, expected, epsilon=0.0001) → float comparison
- waitForCondition(condition, timeoutMs?, intervalMs?) → async polling (replaces setTimeout)
- generateDoc(lineCount) → N-line variable chain markdown
- generateInlineDoc(solveCount) → inline-solve markdown
- benchmarkFn(fn, iterations?, warmup?) → timing harness
- expectNumberValue(value, expected, epsilon?) → typed number assertion

## Async Patterns
- ALWAYS use waitForCondition() instead of setTimeout for async assertions
- All async operations MUST have timeouts (default 1000ms)
- No non-deterministic operations (Date.now, Math.random without seeding)

## Test Structure
- One test file per module or bug
- Bug regressions: Issue{NNN}_shortDescription.spec.ts — must fail if bug re-introduced
- Benchmarks live in __tests__/benchmarks/ as Jest specs
- Tests mirror source structure under __tests__/

## Naming
- describe('Module feature', () => { ... })
- it('does expected thing', () => { ... })
- Bug tests: describe('IssueNNN_description', ...)

## What to Test
- Unit: public API contracts, edge cases, error paths
- Integration: full parseDocument() pipeline, variable deps, cache invalidation
- Regression: one test per GitHub issue
- Benchmarks: performance with statistical rigour

## Golden Rules
- Every new feature needs a test
- Every bug fix gets a regression test
- Tests are deterministic
- Float comparison always uses expectApproximately()
